corrections.source_says: met: the Ideas, Support, & Development (Evidence) rubric explicitly rewards originality and depth of ideas in the produced essay. Two university writing consultants scored this category, and Table 4 reports its arm means as Idea Support. This is an output-based mixed originality/support measure, not a standalone overall-creativity scale; it is sufficient to retain the randomized people study for screening. The sample-size criterion still fails.

corrections.form_value: Randomized lab experiment with 24 people analyzed across three arms (8 per arm; pp. 2-3, 6), well below 50, so criterion 2 fails and the paper goes to the screening report as a small randomized experiment. The 'reduced creative expression' result in the abstract is self-reported (post-survey Q.7, p. 15).

confirmed: Read the complete markdown, including references and Appendix A, and checked numerical claims against the PDF. The source is arXiv:2606.00250v1 [cs.CL], dated 29 May 2026, with 17 PDF pages; the title and all four authors match the form (PDF p. 1 and document page count). No proceedings version was read.

One individually randomized, between-group lab experiment assigned students to control, limited LLM access, or unlimited LLM access; sessions were individual and in person in a private room. lab_rct and context_class=none are correct (PDF p. 1, Abstract; p. 3, Section 3.2; p. 12, Appendix A.1).

The randomized count is 24 college students (PDF p. 1, Abstract); recruitment comprised 24 undergraduate and graduate students from 18 majors (p. 2, Section 3.1). Figure 5 explicitly reports 8 participants per group in the observed writing-process data, supporting 24 analyzed people, below 50 (p. 6, caption; p. 3, Table 1). No separate per-arm assignment counts or post-randomization exclusions are reported, so null per-arm n_randomized is appropriate.

The chatbot used Gemini-2.5-Flash; the limited arm allowed at most 3 prompts and instructed responses under 100 words, while the unlimited arm had no prompt cap or restricted output. Both AI arms were instructed not to request the entire essay (PDF pp. 3-4, Section 3.2; p. 13, Appendix A.1.2 and A.2).

The main methods specify an approximately 30-minute session and at least 300 words; condition instructions say around 300 words, at least 3 paragraphs, and allow as much time as needed. Thus approximately 30 minutes is not a hard time limit (PDF p. 3, Section 3.2; pp. 12-13, Appendix A.1.2).

Two university writing consultants independently rated seven rubric dimensions and their grades were averaged. The appendix gives a 1-5 scale and a 30-point maximum for the first six categories; the human-written item is described as an AI-detection proxy (PDF pp. 4-5, Section 4.2 and footnote 2; pp. 16-17, Essay Grading Rubric).

S1-O1 reported percentages match both tables exactly: Control 88.66%, Limited 88.39%, Unlimited 89.38%. Section 5.3 says no significant group differences; no grade SD, numerical test statistic, or p-value is printed (PDF p. 8, Tables 4-5 and Rubric Based Evaluation).

S1-O2 reported Root TTR values match exactly: Control 8.963, Limited 9.4365, Unlimited 9.555. Root TTR is unique words divided by the square root of total words within an essay, not diversity across writers; no SD or numerical comparison test is printed (PDF p. 5, Section 4.2, Lexical Diversity; p. 8, Table 5 and Section 5.3).

S1-O3 reported cosine similarities match exactly: Control has no value, Limited 0.444, Unlimited 0.552; ANOVA p = 0.21. The comparison uses each essay and that participant's session-specific LLM responses, with all-MiniLM-L6-v2 embeddings, not pairs of different participants' essays (PDF p. 5, Section 4.2, AI Similarity Scores; p. 8, Table 5 and Section 5.3).

All numerical values in the one-line finding match the cited PDF passages. The higher unlimited-arm cosine similarity is descriptive; the paper explicitly says this difference is not statistically significant (PDF p. 8, Tables 4-5 and Section 5.3).

Reduced creative expression is self-report in post-survey Q.7, while creative writing ability and perceived originality are also self-assessed in Q.17 and Q.19. These survey items do not themselves satisfy output-scoring eligibility (PDF p. 15, Post-Interaction Survey).

Appendix A is included on PDF pp. 12-17 and contains the study procedure, consent and instructions, system prompt, survey instruments, and grading rubric. No external supplement or public data/code repository is identified in the text or PDF links; participant data were held in a private Google Drive folder (p. 12, Appendix A.1). This is a primary experiment, not a synthesis (pp. 3-9, Sections 3-8).
summary: The 24-person randomized lab study includes expert scoring of originality within its idea-support rubric, so the output criterion is met, although the sample remains below 50 people. The version, participant counts, and reported numbers match the PDF, but the form overlooks that rubric criterion in its eligibility rationale and task classification and omits the Idea Support and word-count outcomes.
